prize_parts.citation: for the theoretical prediction of flat electronic bands at a magic twist angle in bilayer graphene and the experimental discovery of correlated insulating and superconducting states in twisted bilayer graphene, opening the field of moire quantum materials

statement.case_for: I keep magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene first. After the full exchange I think the scientific case is unchanged and, if anything, better delineated: the Bistritzer-MacDonald continuum model made a specific, checkable prediction (velocity renormalisation to zero and flat bands at a magic angle), and the 2018 experiments found correlated insulators and superconducting domes at that angle in a gate-tunable device. Independent groups with different architectures have since reproduced the main phenomenology, and the same flat-band mechanism has carried into other graphene multilayers and TMD moire systems. That breadth is what separates a new platform for correlated quantum matter from a single result. The allocation of two theory names and one experimental name mirrors the structure of the discovery, and the citation I propose rests on the prediction and the discovery, not on the unresolved pairing mechanism. I have taken the chair's questions seriously, and the honest summary is that B012 is the more mature and cleaner-credited ballot, so my choice of B042 is a judgement about which discovery matters more, not a claim that it is the safer one. I would be content with a B012 outcome and I name it as my first alternative.
statement.case_against: The main weaknesses are the ones the B012 supporters have pressed. The superconducting mechanism and the nature of the correlated insulators are still debated, twist-angle disorder limits sample-to-sample reproducibility, and the experimental credit is concentrated on the group leader while the first author, Yuan Cao, and the Dean, Young, Yacoby, Efetov and Yazdani groups sit outside three names. Lopes dos Santos, Peres and Castro Neto also had an earlier continuum model, though without the magic-angle flat-band result that gives Bistritzer and MacDonald their claim. Against that, B012 is mature, quantitatively cross-checked at the 1e-18 level by several national laboratories, and has the cleanest credit on the shortlist. If the committee weighs maturity and clean attribution above novelty of physical regime, B012 is the right answer and I would not argue against it.

responses.point: Kroll ranks optical lattice clocks first on quantitative, repeated, cross-laboratory evidence, with the cleanest two-name credit, and asks how much a metrology prize can repeat a subfield after 2005 and 2012.
responses.response: I accept your standard of evidence and I think B012 meets it better than B042 does; the 1e-18 comparisons across JILA, RIKEN, PTB, NIST, SYRTE and NPL are exactly the independent agreement I would like to see. On your overlap question, I think a citation built on the magic-wavelength lattice and its realisation is defensible as distinct from the comb and ion-control prizes, because it concerns trapping and interrogating many neutral atoms with the light shift cancelled. But I do not think the overlap is nothing: the 2005 and 2012 prizes already cover the neighbourhood, whereas twisted bilayers open a regime that no earlier prize touches. So we differ on weight, not on facts. What would shift me toward B012 is a clear statement from you and Lindroth that the early lattice-clock groups (Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow) do not have a priority claim that would displace Ye; I cannot assess that from my own field and would defer to you.

responses.point: Lindroth, as an atomic physicist, ranks B012 first with two names and distinct roles (concept and record realisation), and asks colleagues from other areas to test her view; she regards B042 as slightly early because the pairing mechanism is unresolved.
responses.response: You asked to be tested, and my test is mostly a concession. Your account of the credit, with Katori for the magic-wavelength concept and Ye for the record realisation and comparisons, is clearer than anything I can say for B042, and I agree the SI second need not be redefined first, since the redefinition follows from the discovery and not the other way round. On your maturity point about the pairing mechanism, I would still say that what must be settled is the discovery, not the explanation: the cuprates were honoured before their mechanism was known. Where I think you are right is that a mechanism still debated eight years on is a legitimate reason for some colleagues to wait, and I do not think the committee should hide that in the citation. I would be glad to hear whether you would accept B042 in a later cycle if B012 were chosen now, since that bears on whether the two are really competitors.

responses.point: Mehlig ranks B042 first for the minimal Bistritzer-MacDonald model, asks whether Lopes dos Santos, Peres and Castro Neto should share or precede the credit, and questions the theory-heavy two-plus-one split.
responses.response: I share your view of the model as the part of the story to trust most. On priority, I read the earlier Lopes dos Santos, Peres and Castro Neto work as an important precursor on twisted-bilayer band structure, but the sharp statement that the Fermi velocity vanishes and the bands flatten at a specific magic angle is Bistritzer and MacDonald's, and it is that statement the experiments tested. I would therefore keep the credit as proposed and word the citation around the prediction of flat bands, so that we do not imply that the precursor was never made. On the split, I am less worried than you: the experimental discovery has one team leader and the group is credited by the citation wording, but I concede that this leaves Cao outside, and I would not claim the allocation is airtight.

responses.point: Danielsson ranks B042 first but says he would not be embarrassed by a B012 outcome, and notes that the field is only eight years past the key experiment and the origin of superconductivity is still debated.
responses.response: We are close, and I agree with your framing that a B012 outcome would not be an embarrassment. Where I would push back slightly is on the idea that eight years makes B042 hasty: the discovery has been reproduced and extended by independent groups, and the risk that the interpretation reverses is mostly in the superconducting pairing, which our citation does not claim to explain. I would still accept your point that this is the main risk in the proposal. If you and Mehlig agree, I would suggest the three of us state plainly in the final record that B012 is the fallback we would accept, so the split does not look like disagreement about whether the physics is real.

responses.point: Johansson moved from circuit QED to B012 after the openings and flags a possible conflict on B005, B020 and B019, while having ranked B042 sixth because of twist-angle disorder and an unstable interpretation.
responses.response: I noted your move to B012 and your recusal flag on B005. For the record, I agree that a second superconducting-circuit prize one year after the 2025 prize is hard to justify, and I considered that overlap as chair then, so I do not keep B005 in my configuration or alternatives. On twist-angle disorder, I agree it is the sharpest practical objection to B042: it limits sample-to-sample reproducibility, but the central observations have appeared in devices from several groups, so I read it as a limit on precision rather than on whether the phenomenon exists. I leave B030 only as a second alternative, since the credit problem I raised in round 1, with Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang, and the 2016 prize overlap, have not been answered.

uncertainties: Whether the committee judges the pairing mechanism in twisted bilayer graphene to be part of the discovery or an open follow-up, and how much that weighs against B012.

Whether the experimental credit can be defended with one experimental name when Cao, Dean, Young, Yacoby and Efetov fall outside, and whether the precursor continuum model of Lopes dos Santos, Peres and Castro Neto should alter the theory credit.

Whether the early lattice-clock groups (Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow, Pal'chikov) have a priority claim that I cannot judge from outside atomic physics, and how much the 2005 and 2012 prizes should count against B012.
Whether B030 attribution (Kane, Mele, Molenkamp versus Bernevig, Hughes, Zhang and the 3D pioneers) can be resolved fairly under a three-name limit.
statement.conflict_note: No new conflict. I am a theoretical condensed-matter physicist working on first-principles electronic structure and magnetism, with no collaboration with the credited candidates on B042, B012 or B030. I chaired the committee for the 2025 prize on superconducting-circuit macroscopic quantum tunnelling, and I have weighed the overlap with B005; since B005 is not in my configuration it does not require recusal. I defer to Lindroth and Kroll on atomic physics and metrology.
